newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian democracy under spotlight in local poll.
newsitem.headline: Albanian democracy under spotlight in local poll.

text.p: Albanian democracy comes under international scrutiny for the second time in five months on Sunday when the voters take part in nationwide local elections.

A disputed general election spread over May and June was widely criticised by Western governments and on Wednesday a branch of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) decided not to monitor Sunday's voting after the government approved only part of its list of observers.

The United States and the 15-nation European Union have sent a clear signal to the conservative government of President Sali Berisha that they will be watching closely this weekend for signs of Albania's commitment to democracy.

"The local elections are extremely important so that the world can see Albania carrying out a nationwide election that meets international standards," a senior Council of Europe official said during a recent visit to Albania.
The 39-nation Council of Europe, which promotes democracy and human rights, expressed reservations over the results of the general election, which was boycotted by most opposition groups.

The Socialist Party, the former communists, and other opposition parties accused Berisha's ruling Democrats of rigging the vote and intimidating their supporters. The Democrats secured 89 percent of the vote.
The United States and Italy have publicly called on Berisha to hold a new general election as soon as possible.
The OSCE came out strongly against the conduct of the spring poll, saying it did not meet international standards.

That report angered Berisha and the Democrats. The government subsequently has refused to accept the full list of monitors from the OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) for the local polls, prompting fresh concern over Albania's adherence to democratic rules.
"The number of observers for any election observation mission is not a matter for negotiation with the host government," the ODIHR said in a statement on Wednesday.
Council of Europe observers had already arrived in the Balkan state, where communism was toppled in December 1990.
Some 2.2 million Albanians are eligible to vote in the elections for councils at town, district and communal level.
The toughest fight is expected in Tirana where all parties have put forward heavyweight candidates for the crucial post of Tirana mayor, held by the Democrats for the last four years.

The Democrats are fielding Albert Brojka, who stepped down as construction minister to run for mayor. The Socialists are backing Agim Fagu, the country's best-known basketball player, who is standing as an independent.
Even party leaders, such as Neritan Ceka of the centre-right Democratic Alliance and Petrit Kalakulla of the Democratic Party of the Right, are standing for mayor.
Brojka told a rally in a rundown Tirana suburb that he would fight to improve power and water supplies and proposed a ring road around the city to relieve traffic congestion.
Fagu said: "Tirana can be only be governed better by the opposition. The inefficiency and nepotism of the central government affects Tirana more than anywhere else."
In the last local polls in July 1992, the Socialists won more town halls than the Democrats but the governing party took all the big cities, including Durres, Shkoder, Fier and Vlore.
The Democrats also won by 43.5 percent of district councils to the Socialists' 41 percent, but the former communists won slightly more support in the communal vote.
Final results were expected by the middle of next week.
